author: Humanread Founder

chapters.html:
Beside the Willow

Ahe settled into Grandpa Song's boat with a stage sword. It was safely inside its scabbard, on its way to the theatre ahead. He did not draw it to play.

Grandpa Song sat at the stern with an oar. On the left bank stood a forked willow, with a large white stone at its roots. Farther to the right was their landing dock.

Ahe looked ahead, thinking of the busy stage. Willow branches hung above spreading ripples. He moved the prop from his knees to the wood beside him, without noticing how close it was to the edge.
chapters.title: Beside the Willow

chapters.html:
After the Splash

The boat rocked gently. The sheathed sword slipped over the side. “Oh!” Ahe reached, too late. A splash broke the surface, then left a few widening rings.

The sword sank and came to rest on the riverbed near the willow and white stone. From the boat, only shifting light showed on the water.

Ahe stayed inside; he did not jump after it. He stared at the piece of wood where it had fallen. “I must remember this spot,” he thought, “so I can find it again.”
chapters.title: After the Splash

chapters.html:
A Reassuring Little Mark

Ahe did not look again at the willow or remember the stone on the bank. With a small pebble, he scratched one short mark in the wooden side of the boat.

“It fell from right here.” He measured the scratch with his finger and felt relieved. “At the dock, I'll look below this mark.”

The scratch did mark the right piece of wood. But Ahe forgot to ask whether that wood would remain above the same patch of river. Below the water, the sword stayed where it had landed.
chapters.title: A Reassuring Little Mark

chapters.html:
The Mark Takes a Ride

The boat continued to the right. The willow and white stone stayed on the left bank, while the dock drew closer. Ahe looked down. The scratch was still in front of him.

He felt reassured. He had not noticed that the mark was travelling with the plank. It marked a place on the boat, not a place on the riverbed.

The boat covered more water, but the sword did not make that journey. It remained on the bottom. The gap between boat and sword grew wider.
chapters.title: The Mark Takes a Ride

chapters.html:
Nothing Below the Mark

At the dock, Ahe immediately looked into the water below the scratch. Light shimmered beside the boat, but there was no sword. “The mark is still here. Where did it go?”

Tao was on the dock. After hearing what had happened, she pointed left toward the willow. “You said it fell when you passed that tree, didn't you?” Grandpa Song nodded in the same direction.

Ahe raised his eyes. The white stone was still beside the distant willow, but the boat was now at the dock. “I travelled with the boat. The sword didn't.” The scratch had not vanished; it was simply above a different place.
chapters.title: Nothing Below the Mark

chapters.html:
A Different Way to Look

Grandpa Song tied up the boat. Ahe stepped ashore, and the three walked left along the broad bank. Tao stayed on the inner, grassy side. They were going back to look near the willow and stone. Nobody entered the water.

Ahe's hands were empty. Understanding his mistake had not magically brought the sword back. This time, though, he knew to look at the landmarks on shore rather than the mark moving with the boat.

The saying about marking a boat to find a sword warns against keeping an unsuitable method when circumstances have changed. A lasting mark is not always a useful one. First ask what has moved and what has stayed; then decide how to adjust.

Adapted from the saying in Master Lü's Spring and Autumn Annals, Examining the Present. The recurring cast, stage prop and return along the bank follow episode four of this original children's series. The river is drawn in cutaway so readers can see the resting place; the characters cannot see through the water.
chapters.title: A Different Way to Look

summary: A stage sword sinks beside a willow, but Ahe marks the boat instead of remembering the shore. At the dock, his mark is still there. Where is the sword? Six illustrated scenes about noticing what moves and what stays.
title: Tao's Story Garden: The Mark on the Boat
